summary: For ages 6–7, teach counting on for addition and counting back for subtraction as the efficiency step beyond counting-all. The core skills: start from the larger number (e.g. begin at 8 for 8+3), say the NEXT number as the first count ('9'), and track the number of steps so the start isn't miscounted. Best anchored on a visible number line/track where hops are seen and counted, then gradually replaced by known and derived facts. Target sums: 8+3=11 (count on), 12−3=9 (count back), 2+9 (start from the larger addend, 9).
misconceptions: Counting all from one instead of counting on from a number (a normal earlier stage).
Counting the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → 8,9,10 = 10), an off-by-one error.
Counting on from the first-written number rather than the larger one, making more steps than needed.
Counting in the wrong direction for subtraction.
Over-relying on counting for facts that should become instant recall.

activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
steps: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.insight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.

activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start
steps: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.insight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.

activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
steps: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.insight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.

checkQuestion: Work these out and show me how you count each one: 8 + 3; 12 − 3; 6 + 2.
checkAnswer: 11; 9; 8. Watch for the child counting ON from the larger number (starting at 8, saying '9, 10, 11'), counting BACK for the subtraction, and NOT counting the start number as a step.
